entries.title: Discord Rewrites Desktop and Mobile Clients in Rust Using Zed's GPU-Accelerated Rendering Framework
entries.summary: Discord’s CTO Stanislav Vishnevskiy recently announced rewriting its desktop and mobile clients in Rust, moving away from Electron and React Native. The project eliminates layers of abstraction to directly leverage the device’s GPU, native mobile views, and a Rust core shared across platforms. Early results hint at a significant reduction in RAM usage and boot time for chat, voice, and streaming.
entries.content:
Discord’s CTO Stanislav Vishnevskiy recently announced rewriting its desktop and mobile clients in Rust, moving away from Electron and React Native. The project (codenamed Phoenix) eliminates layers of abstraction to directly leverage the device’s GPU, native mobile views, and a Rust core shared across platforms. Early results hint at a significant reduction in RAM usage and boot time for chat, voice, and streaming.

Vishnevskiy expanded on the rewrite on X:

We’ve been early adopters of Rust since 2018 and a lot of our infra, voice tech, and even some of the current client is already Rust, the holy grail was getting the whole client there. That means Electron goes away, and so does React Native, mobile keeps native UI but shares app code with desktop via Rust. We hope to get it into testing with users soon™. (And it’s not Tauri, it’s GPUI, so good guess everyone.)

The desktop app thus drops Chromium/Node.js for GPUI, the open-source, GPU-accelerated Rust UI framework built by the Zed team for the Zed editor. Zed is an open-source code editor written in Rust for macOS, Linux, and Windows by a team including the creators of GitHub’s Atom code editor, which was sunsetted in 2022, four years after Microsoft’s acquisition of GitHub. Zed touts a narrow focus on performance and user (i.e., developer) experience:

VS Code won by being good enough for everyone. Zed wins by being excellent for developers who refuse to compromise on speed.

Discord’s mobile app rewrite drops React Native, instead directly leveraging native iOS and Android views and reusing a common Rust core.

The browser client keeps rendering HTML with the application logic layer compiled to WebAssembly. Embedded web surfaces (e.g., YouTube videos and Activities), however, invoke an OS webview, with Electron’s built-in browser no longer available.

Vishnevskiy signals decreasing RAM usage, startup time, and latency as key motivations behind the rewrite:

The new Discord client using less RAM is just part of the story. Clicking around feels instant, I can’t go back. Check out the boot time.

Early internal builds for the desktop app reveal RAM usage at around 290 MB (measured with two accounts logged in simultaneously) and a near-instant cold start versus 5.5 s on Electron.

Vishnevskiy showcased similar improvements on mobile with a load time under 2 seconds for the rewrite versus approximately 5 seconds for the legacy app.

Elias Floreteng, in his master’s thesis at KTH this year (An Empirical Study of React Native’s New Architecture), reported performance gains across several metrics for native Swift and Kotlin over React Native, even with its new architecture. The controlled benchmark involves a 1,000-row scrollable image list using stock list and image components, with identical assets and row geometry across all binaries. Floreteng concludes that Swift beats React Native across every comparable runtime metric on iOS. On Android, the gap to native is small and runs in both directions, with native ahead on memory and CPU.

On desktop, Zed proved that leveraging GPUI could provide better performance over Electron and alternative frameworks reusing the device’s native webview (e.g., Tauri).

While Tauri also uses a Rust backend, it leverages the operating system’s native webview. This has the advantage of letting web developers reuse their knowledge of HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, while also avoiding the bundling of Chromium. Executable size is, as a result, generally smaller. Tauri apps’ RAM usage on Windows, however, tends to be similar to that of their Electron counterparts, as the same core, resource-hungry browser technology is used. Webview behavior may also be inconsistent across operating systems.

GPUI replaces the browser engine with a hybrid immediate and retained mode, GPU-accelerated UI framework that targets 120-frames-per-second rendering without garbage-collection pauses. In exchange for the reported performance gains, developers give up many rendering and accessibility features that come baked into the browser (e.g., text layout, input method integration, screen-reader accessibility hooks, right-to-left support). While miscellaneous Rust libraries exist to address some of these issues (e.g., Parley for text layout), developers still have to wire them into a consistent user experience.

entries.title: LinkedIn Cuts Daily Spark Shuffle Fetch Failures from 750 to 20 with Apache Celeborn
entries.summary: LinkedIn deployed Apache Celeborn as a shared remote shuffle platform across most Spark and Flink workloads, reducing daily shuffle fetch failures from approximately 750 to 20. The deployment also lowered compute costs by 10%, improved application runtimes by 14%, and reduced shuffle costs per task by nearly 90% through dedicated storage, replication, and data-plane optimizations. By Leela Kumili
entries.content:
LinkedIn has deployed Apache Celeborn as a shared remote shuffle platform across the majority of its Apache Spark and Apache Flink workloads, separating intermediate data storage from compute infrastructure. The deployment reduces daily shuffle fetch failures from approximately 750 to 20, lowers compute costs by 10%, and improves application runtimes by 14%, compared with its previous Magnet implementation.

Daily shuffle fetch failures decreased from approximately 750 to 20 (Source: LinkedIn Blog Post)

LinkedIn's offline data platform executes more than 300,000 Spark jobs daily across thousands of production nodes, consuming approximately 200 petabyte-hours of compute. As the company moves toward a unified Flink architecture for real-time and historical processing, large-scale backfills introduce additional shuffle workloads. Shuffle moves intermediate data between processing stages, potentially stressing networks, disks, and application runtimes.

LinkedIn previously addressed shuffle read inefficiencies with Magnet, its push-based shuffle implementation contributed to Apache Spark 3.2. Magnet aggregates shuffle blocks by reducer partition into larger files, reducing random disk reads. However, shuffle storage remained within the compute cluster, where External Shuffle Services shared CPU, memory, disk I/O, and network resources with compute workloads.

With Apache Celeborn, map tasks push intermediate data to dedicated workers, which aggregate and store partitions independently of compute executors. Reducers fetch the data directly from these workers, allowing shuffle storage to scale independently of compute and reducing dependence on executor lifecycles. Unlike Magnet, which uses merger External Shuffle Services within the Spark compute cluster, Celeborn runs as a separate shuffle service with dedicated workers and a replicated control plane. This separation reduces resource contention between compute and shuffle workloads.

Celeborn architecture at LinkedIn (Source: LinkedIn Blog Post)

Aravind Patnam, a staff software engineer at LinkedIn, explained,

Operating it reliably across thousands of nodes and hundreds of thousands of daily applications required substantial engineering beyond the upstream project.

The deployment uses a five-node Raft-based control plane distributed across availability zones, with Apache Ratis providing metadata replication, leader election, and failover. LinkedIn also introduced network-aware replication and integrated Celeborn with its host health platform to deprioritize workers approaching maintenance and exclude degraded workers. These changes contributed to a 20-fold reduction in task failures during infrastructure disruptions compared with Magnet.

LinkedIn further optimized the data plane by moving shuffle storage to NVMe SSDs, reducing overall shuffle duration by 40%. Using Zstandard compression instead of LZ4 reduced the required shuffle worker fleet by approximately 35%. The company also provisioned workers with 100 Gbps network interfaces and improved slot selection time sixfold through JVM and data-plane optimizations. Across the fleet, shuffle cost decreased by nearly 90% per task, while the proportion of executor runtime spent waiting on shuffle operations fell by approximately 10–15% from its peak.

The converged Flink platform processes hundreds of millions of events per hour in historical backfills, completing multi-day workloads in single-digit hours. Thousands of pipelines now use unified Flink computations for nearline processing and historical corrections, replacing parallel Spark implementations. LinkedIn is exploring caching and faster upstream upgrades while continuing to contribute to Celeborn.

entries.title: Presentation: Behind Booking.com's AI Evolution: The Unpolished Story
entries.summary: Jabez Eliezer Manuel discusses the 20-year evolution of Booking.com’s data management and ML platforms. He explains how they scaled MySQL topologies, sunset Hadoop for cloud architecture, and built high-throughput model serving and feature stores operating at 400B predictions per day. He also shares insights on personalization, interleaved experimentation, and their new agentic AI foundation. By J
entries.content:
Transcript

Jabez Eliezer Manuel: Today, Booking.com impacts billions of travel decisions, and behind each of those travel decisions is actually a bunch of ML platforms working behind the scenes. I'm here to talk about them. In the spirit of QCon's 20th anniversary, we are going to go back in time by two decades and take on a journey and then see how these platforms evolve.

To make it easier for you to follow along, I've structured my talk into three layers, the data management layer, the ML engineering, and domain intelligence. In the data management layer, we will see the evolution of our databases, and some of the scale challenges that we had, and the cloud migration that we undertook to actually better our data. In the ML engineering layer, it'll be model serving at scale, and our feature engineering atoms there. In the domain intelligence layer, it'll be a high-level tour of all the machine learning platforms that we have. I'll pick one of them and then do a deep dive, so you get a full evolution of that specific platform, and you'll also have something tangible to take.

The World in 2005

Let's go back to 2005. This was how the world looked like in 2005, if you remember these camera phones. Web 2.0 was taking off as a platform, and Booking.com was just like 9 years old. It had still not joined the Priceline group. Inside Booking, something fascinating was happening. We had run our first A/B experiment. Today everything goes through experimentation. It doesn't matter if it's a simple CSS change or an infrastructure change, everything goes through experimentation. At any point in time, if you're visiting Booking.com, you are subjected to 1,000-plus experiments, literally. Over the period of time, we have run 150,000 experiments or more until now. One thing that's certain is that most of our experiments fail, our success rate is just less than 25%. The goal isn't to get it right, but it is to learn fast. If you see that golden star on the top right, it's my little takeaway marker.

It's my way of hinting to you that there might be a lesson in this slide that is reusable for you. Continuing on experimentation. Experimentation built our data-driven DNA. It gave us a lot of technical benefits, which is sure. The ones that I like are that it eliminated HIPPOs. There were no endless debates internally. You just say, ok, let's go and build, test it, and done. The last is like, no, it created a culture of humility. There were no experts in the room, meaning that nobody could pinpoint and say, yes, let's experiment and then figure it out.

Data Management Layer

Experiments needed data, and that's where we are going to begin our journey in data management. In this part, I want to talk about our MySQL, our Hadoop, and our move to cloud. These are the three topics that I want to cover. This was our original tech stack when Booking.com started. It was just Perl and Postgres. Quickly, we replaced Postgres with MySQL, primarily because of its asynchronous replication capabilities and for other reasons as well. In 2005, our setup was just a single master and four slaves. Fast forward 15 years, we were operating one of the largest clusters in the world. You might be wondering, how do you manage so many instances? Three things. We have a single writer setup, and we have replication chains, which I'll show you. Then we have a lot of automation. Let's make it real with an example, with an image. What you're seeing is a single master topology.

On the left, orange is the master, and then there are replicas or slaves. The colors indicate different data centers out there. As you can see, we minimize the replication across DCs by having intermediate masters. This whole topology is managed by a replication management tool called Orchestrator. If anybody is using MySQL, you might be aware of it. Automation was a necessity. For example, every 60 days, we take these 7,000 instances or so out, deprovision them, and reprovision them again. That meant that for every three minutes, there is some action that is going on. It is not humanely possible for some engineer to sit and do it. We have plenty of automation to do that.

There are a few things that makes our MySQL setup a little bit different. One is we don't use any specialized hardware. It's like simple frontend blades that are used for MySQL. No stored procedures, no UDFs, no views, not even a cache layer. Yes, no cache layers. The secret sauce, what we do is we actually create smaller DBs. The soft limit is 2 terabytes. The hard limit is 10 terabytes. We try to keep everything small. The reason is we want this database to fit into the fast storage of that server blade that we are using. In this example, we were normally using server blade 7 or 9, if you are aware of its configuration. What that meant is our point queries were less than 350 microseconds, which was roughly in the order of some of the memory engines out there. We were effectively using MySQL as a cache.

It also provided several side benefits. It was faster backups, quicker failovers, and primarily also lower cost, because if you're moving away from fast storage to iSCSI, it's expensive. We didn't just use MySQL. We actually helped shape it. What do I mean by that? In the early days of Booking, we had expertise in-house to fork MySQL, but we made a conscious decision to say that we're not going to fork, we're going to contribute upstream. Many of the features that you see today exist because we wanted it. Like, for example, GTID-based replication is because we actually proposed it. We made the case. We shaped the design of MySQL.

I want to sidestep a bit and then give you a picture of how machine learning looked in that era. It was Perl scripts and statistical and scientific computing libraries from CPAN and just cron jobs. The deployment strategy was simple. Copy the script and pray. It solved real business problems. We were able to do fraud detection. We were doing demand forecasting with regression. We were doing recommendations with KNN and a few other things. Even in those days, we were able to solve that. This MySQL setup helped us a bit. As data grew large, we needed something more. Hadoop came to the rescue. In 2011, we actually built two on-premise clusters. This was a configuration that was there. It was redundant clusters. The setup looked like this. There was MySQL on bare metal. Then there was this classic Hadoop stack, HDFS, YARN, MapReduce. Then we layered it with Oozie for orchestration, Spark for workflows, and Hive for SQL, and Sqoop for moving data between Hadoop and MySQL.

On top of it, we had some self-serve tooling, a classic setup. Data came into Hadoop via two means. From MySQL, it came as nightly jobs into Hadoop. Then from Kafka, it was Kafka Connect that was bringing in data. This data was used for machine learning purposes. This is how prediction training was happening back then. What you see is two workflows, the training workflow on the top and an inference workflow. A scientist would actually write a workflow where they would train a Python model. Then they call it as pickling the model, which is just serializing the model, storing into Hadoop. Then another workflow loads that model, does the prediction that it wants. Then it actually stores it into MySQL in some cases, but not in all cases. Basically, the whole prediction was happening completely offline. In some cases, we want real-time. In those cases, what we did was we just faked it.

This is how we faked it. The top is the offline workflow, and the bottom is a web request. We wanted the real-time prediction to happen in the web request. All we did was we trained the model. I'll give you an example how we did it. Let's take an example of a model that we want to train, like device and country is the feature, and probability to book is the output that we want to do. In those cases, what we did was we just enumerated all the input features. We just created all possible devices, all possible countries. Then we just predicted on that upfront. That gave us a table. All we did was store that table into the MySQL. Then when the request came in, we just queried the table as if we were predicting, and then went on to do our job. Obviously, it doesn't work for most cases, but that was our earlier real-time prediction with faking it with lookup tables.

That worked for us in most cases. Hadoop powered for us most of our pipeline for many years, but there were some problems. One was it was a shared environment, so every training, production workloads, everything was running in a single cluster. There was mono-version. If you are a data scientist, you cannot use a version that you want. You just have to use a version that is possible, like now it is shared. The second thing was there was no GPU support. That limited our ability to train a bigger model, larger model. We were using two different DCs for redundant setup. Then you need to keep the data in sync between this, and that was becoming a headache. Capacity issues, like at peak times, we were operating very close to max capacity. Noisy neighbors, like some NOOB who's writing a query can actually clog the entire production cluster.

Most importantly, there was no discovery or ownership, even though people depended on each other's data. That was the biggest headache for us. This is what it looked like. Like now somebody might think that this is a Rorschach psychological test, but it is just a dependency graph for our workflows. If you zoom in closely, you can see Hadoop screaming in binary there.

2011, we introduced Hadoop. 2018, we realized the limitation of Hadoop, but then it took us until 2022 to put it into maintenance mode, and another three years to go into sunset. Like now what was going wrong? Why did it take so long, that hairball that you saw earlier? Why was it difficult? We were operating with hundreds of petabytes of data. We had about 190,000 Hadoop tables, 7,000-plus workflows, hundreds of teams, and then we want to keep everything up and running. Our goal was move everything, stop nothing, align everyone. Everybody knows that that last part is already a moonshot. We were like, why pick one impossible thing? Pick three. We had four problems to solve. One was, we wanted to actually modernize our compute and scale it, obviously, because we were operating at max capacity. Then we want segregation of workflows, because we wanted isolation at least between dev and production.

Governance and ownership, which was a mess, we wanted to fix that. The last was, we wanted to enable discovery of workflows and datasets so that people can reuse things. Saying goodbye to Hadoop was hard, and this is why. This is what happened in those gap years. 2018, when we realized the mistake, or realized the problem, we actually attempted to move into one of the cloud providers. Quickly, the product got shelved. The reason was, depending upon who you ask, it is either cost or a strategy shift. We quickly pivoted to building something internally to help us. Like now we actually built assistant application along with Hadoop to have a data catalog. Then we also had built Kubernetes clusters to do Spark. That eased us a little bit, so we could continue on. A short bit later, we started the modernization project, where we focused on three things, like quality, ownership, and governance of data.

We were trying to fix that with that modernization project. During that time period, we actually piloted another cloud, and that showed promise, but we didn't actually make enough to move the needle to actually do a full migration. In 2023, leadership actually made the call, and they said, guys, we're going to do it all in, no plan B. That actually helped, we made progress, and we succeeded. Just within one and a half years, we migrated everything that you saw. This is how we did it. Maybe there is something in there for you. We actually built a tool that mapped every possible table, every dependency into a graph. That was our first effort, map the universe. Second thing that we did was, we looked at the usage analysis of all the tables and the workflows, and the lineage as well, and said, which of this is business critical?

Then we tried to trim it down. You'd be surprised that 92% of the workflows didn't pass the test, someone cares, it was easy. The best architectural tool is Delete key. What we then did is, we actually did graph analysis on those workflows that passed, and we actually prioritized it by centrality and impact. We took a few, and after that it was simple. Group them into batches, do the migration, and slowly phase out the legacy system.

If you look back, one key thing that made the difference was this unified command center, which held that graph data, and that became the central place for anybody to look at it during the migration. If I had a workflow that I had to migrate, but then I depended on a few other workflows, I could go in there and then see, ok, when is my dependency migrating, and when can I migrate. I could plan things easy. Anything, status, dependencies, blockers, everything was in there. This replaced spreadsheet tracking, and also it replaced tribal knowledge. Everybody knew what exactly was happening. The second thing we already saw was, we removed plan B out of the equation. Leadership said, just go in. We all know that this is not always the best plan. The best strategy is prevention. If we had a time machine, these are the four messages that we would send to our past self. First, catalog every asset that you have. Data workflows doesn't matter. Catalog it. Establish clear ownership. It can be business ownership and also technical ownership of the data. Build quality gates before you share that data. Track lineage end-to-end. That concludes our data layer.

ML Engineering Layer

Next in the ML engineering layer, I want to talk about two things. One is how we industrialized ML model serving. Second, our attempts at feature engineering and the problem that still remains. Before I do that, I want to give you a 30-second overview of evolution of our ML stack. In 2005, we actually were using Perl libraries and the MySQL, which was still doing the job. Hadoop came into the picture that brought in big data analysis and reporting, that was good. True machine learning kickstarted with the introduction of Oozie and Python, like the sklearn era, because we were able to do things easily. When Spark came in, that changed the game or changed the pace of the game. Now we were able to do more things faster and we were able to crunch more numbers. H2O took it to another level. Now we were able to do faster training.

Also, we were able to deploy models directly in any Java environment. That was a big thing. In 2017, deep learning came in. Deep learning started as a very simple hackathon project, where a group of developers wanted to improve the image stacks, which was of low quality. From then on, it is widely adopted across the company. 2023, LLM wave took off and we built a bunch of generative products, which we'll touch upon a bit later. 2025, we started laying the foundations of the agentic systems, which we'll also touch later.

Going back, if you look at the timeline, 2015, in my opinion, was a pivotal year, because we were solving two problems. One was real-time predictions. Until then, we were solving real-time predictions with fake lookup tables that you saw earlier. In a hackathon, we actually built a small Scala service, which was backed by a storage. It was actually used to do model serving. Machine learning scientists could upload the model. Back in those days, the model was just classical problems, like logistic regression, classification, and so on. Uploading a model is nothing but uploading a CSV file with all the features that was used, what type of those features, and some weights and coefficients. In real time, when a user landed on the website, some backend service collected the features necessary to invoke the model. Then they used the Perl SDK, because we were still in Perl back then, to invoke the Scala service.

Over a period of time, this Scala service has evolved into a platform. Now it supports 12-plus different model formats. You can think of all the major ones are in here. This is how the setup looks like today. That service is deployed in multiple clusters. Why multiple clusters? We have some general-purpose shared tenant clusters, some dedicated clusters for very critical workloads, and then also some clusters for batch. Either these clusters actually host their model, or they actually can interact with externally hosted models, so like SageMaker. They can also contact feature store, which we'll cover later. To hide the complexity from the end users, these clusters are fronted by a custom proxy. Every prediction that these clusters make, is logged. Then those logs go into data lake and also to our monitoring platforms. Let's take an example how a flow of machine learning scientists uploading a model and inference happens.

Machine learning scientists upload the model artifact into something like S3, and then they notify an ML portal to say, I've registered this new model. That triggers a pipeline. The coordinator goes and picks up that model that the ML scientist uploaded, and then comes back, versions it in its own storage. Also, what it does is, it finds the right cluster to deploy, and then allocates enough space, and triggers that upload. In addition, it'll also upload that, update the proxy that you saw earlier to say that the proxy knows which cluster to route to. Serving was simple. When a web request came in, backend servers just invoked the custom proxy with this client SDK. This was one of our success stories. There was no problem, and it was a clear success. Two years back, this is what that system that you just saw handled. It has 480-plus models. It can do 400 billion predictions per day. All of those predictions within less than 20 milliseconds on an average. Those are impressive numbers.

Second problem that we started solving in 2015 was feature engineering. Back then, 80% of the time was spent on just data preparation. Two pain points emerged. One was duplication. Each team was trying to build the feature by themselves in a different way. The second was there was skew. The models that behaved one way in training was behaving another way in inference. We set out to solve the problem by solving the duplication and to bring consistency. We thought, let's build reusable computations. We decided to tackle the problem separately for offline and for online, because offline was targeted at machine learning scientists. Online was targeted for engineers. I'm going to sidestep here to give you the context so you can better understand the decisions that the team made. What you're seeing on screen is just an initial dataset. You have a user ID, what the user searched and when.

Then also the label that we are predicting on to say that did the user eventually book or not. That's the initial dataset. That's how an ML scientist starts their work. What they do is they try to add more features into this dataset. They keep looking for other feature tables. Feature tables look like this, which is just a time series representation of a feature. In this case, the feature represented is what is the number of searches that the user did in the last seven days. That is the series that you're seeing. Once they found such a feature table, all they do is a point-in-wise join, wherein they take a unique ID, in this case, user ID, and some timestamp, and they do a time-wise join on it. Then they get a training set, wherein they have the feature that they were looking for, which in this case is the count of last seven days.

When we looked at this, we said, we can help in two places. One is building that feature table, and the other is doing the time-wise join. That is what we set out to achieve. That was a feature table. That feature table is built by another fact log or an immutable log. This is just the searches that have happened over a period of time. By looking at this, it is just very clear that there is one data frame and the other data frame. We figured out we can actually just use Spark ML transformer, which did the feature translation between.

This is how it looked in its entirety. There were immutable fact logs, which is just log of search events that have happened in the past. We asked people to write reusable feature encoders that converted into a feature table. Once we had that, all anybody has to do is just go look at the initial dataset and do a time-wise join on it. We tried to do something similar to online as well. There were event streams. We asked people to write feature mappers in Scala, and that became enriched streams. From there, there was a centralized team which took all these features, put it into Cassandra, and then served it via an API. There were a couple of problems with this approach. One was parity. Data was different between online and offline. The computation was different from online and offline. Then there were performance issues because of the amount of data that we were processing in offline.

Backfilling or recomputation was hard. In the second attempt, we decided, let's fix data and computational parity together. The way we fixed data parity was we introduced the concept of timelines. Timelines is nothing but a time-ordered sequence of events for a user. User searched, user clicked, user booked, things like that. The idea was, let's build this timeline equally or approximately in the same way for both online and offline. Then that way, once we have that, we can just write computation once and then use the timeline. That was a big picture. This is how the timelines were built. Those are the search, clicks, and immutable events. They got materialized into Hadoop. We built timeline builders separately. It's a duplicate effort, but it was managed by a central team. That timeline was operating separately for online and offline. They synced the data or the timelines into Cassandra and HDFS. The only difference between these two timelines were the Cassandra timelines were trimmed. Unlike the MVA, TVA, we actually didn't trim timelines for saving the universe. We trimmed timelines in Cassandra for saving the space.

This is how we used timelines for computational parity. We had a full timeline in HDFS, a trimmed timeline in Cassandra. We asked people to write centralized shared feature libraries. These are things that can be used to compute features, things like sum, count, large scale, and all those typical things was written by a centralized team. It also allowed extension. Anybody could come in and write in the feature that is not already there. In online or in real time, when an application wanted some inference, they would go to a feature store API and ask, can you give me this feature? What it would do is go into Cassandra, pick up the timeline for that specific user or use case, and then build that feature on the fly with these shared libraries. The same happened on the training side or on offline. That stack was Python, because scientists were using Python.

We had a wrapper, which had a feature computation library wrapper. What it did was, whenever the scientist wanted a feature, it submitted a Spark job. In that Spark job, we actually did the same thing. We typically achieved what we wanted to do, both data and feature parity. The problem was, ML scientists were not familiar with writing features in Java, and that created a dependency between engineering and ML science. Secondly, in the previous one, the Cassandra timelines, computing features on the fly was costly, expensive, because it took more than 90 milliseconds or so to actually just fetch the data. It was not suitable for most of the use cases. Then we said, ok, third attempt. Forget feature computation, we'll just focus on feature storage and serving. Let people deal with feature computation. We didn't care how features are computed, as long as we knew where to pick the features from.

If it was pre-computed, ok, we'll go to a data lake of sorts. If it is real time, we'll go to Kafka. Then we built a feature store. In the feature store, there was an ingestor component, which knew about these multiple data sources, and pulled that data, and stored it into an online store, and served it via an API. In this API, there was no on-the-fly computation. It was just a simple lookup, because features were already computed. The same pipeline, what it also did was sync data into offline, so that MLS can use it for retraining purposes, and for also other analysis. This feature store also had other benefits, like it had feature registry, feature monitoring, and so on. In essence, after three attempts, this is what we learned. It's a multidimensional problem, and we don't have an answer. Currently, for the pre-computation and real time, we currently have three systems, and we are always looking for one more system. That wraps the second layer.

Domain Intelligence Layer

Now in that third layer, we are moving away from infrastructure to business impact. I want to give you a high-level tour of all the ML platforms that we have, and then dive into one of them. This is the platform that we have. One is GenAI platform. It's the newest kid in the block. What it does is it enables any team to actually safely build generative AI experiences. It provides tools and infrastructure and foundational capabilities like guardrails, evaluation, orchestration out of the box. Things like PII detection, PII masking, everything comes out of the box. The product teams can focus just on product innovation and not on LLM plumbing. Let's look at a few use cases there, what we have. The trip planning, which is just a conversational experience where someone can go talk in natural language and get recommendations, that's powered by GenAI. We have smart filters.

If you were ever on Booking.com, you would see hundreds of filters on the left, and it is hard for anyone to know which to pick. We have a text box where you can type it, and that translated into the right filters and sorters. The third is review summaries. That provides, based on the last reviews, a quick snapshot of pros and cons. The next is property Q&A. This actually enables instant answers to any property-specific questions, and it is grounded on reviews, past Q&A, and that is also powered by GenAI. We also have a booking support, wherein we have AI that can do basic customer support on payments, cancellation, and things regarding your booking. These are the use cases. There are many interesting things under the platform, but we are not going to cover it today.

GenAI is good, but to generate data, we actually want good content. That's where content intelligence comes in. What it does is it provides surfaces like good, high-quality content that are usable. This platform analyzes every image and text. It actually adds metadata or enriches that metadata. For example, if it is images, it adds themes, tags, and looks for any harmful content. If it is text, it looks for, for example, sentiments or topics that have been discussed. This also supports the reviews. Because most of the things happen in the background, like fraud detection is also taken care of by this content intelligence. One example that you see, anytime you see a gallery on Booking.com, it is probably powered by this content intelligence. Picking up the right photo to put up front and the order, which photos to highlight and so on. The other thing is, it autogenerates all text for screen readers.

There's a platform for that. It also does reviews. It detects topics on the reviews and summarizes it at the property level. This is what it enabled was, not just getting intelligence at content level, but going one level higher. For example, if property had all the images and all the summaries, we can actually create intelligence at the property level to see what is happening. That kind of aggregation level, this platform enabled. The third is ranking. Ranking's responsibility is to order millions of products so that any time a customer comes in, they see the most relevant results for them, like something personalized. This is a platform that we are going to dig in, so I'll park it here. Recommendations is a self-serve platform wherein you can build any kind of recommendations across the funnel, from discovery to post-booking. It has more than 40, 50 use cases. I picked a few to give you a flavor of what it looks like.

The pushcards that you might see on Booking.com is powered by recommendations. There's multi-vertical recommendations. When I say multi-vertical, I'm referring to accommodations, flights, attractions, and so on. Those kinds of recommendations come from this platform. Unique stays, team-based recommendations for you, and attraction carousels that you might see on the page, and any flight recommendations. All of these are examples that are powered by recommendations platform. The last platform is value intelligence. The responsibility of this platform is to measure and optimize promotions. By promotions, I mean anything like vouchers, discounts, things like rewards that's being optimized by value intelligence. The goal of this platform is to say, maximize value for travelers, partners, and the business. That wraps all the platforms.

Let's jump into ranking platform. Ranking is a three-way optimization problem. We need choice and value for customers. We need exposure and growth for the partners. We also need efficiency and revenue for business. If we show irrelevant results, the travelers are going to be annoyed. If we show poor visibility, partners are going to be frustrated. If any one of them is annoyed for too long, I'm going to get my salary re-ranked. It's a three-way optimization problem. Back then in 2005, we had the formula for ranking hotels look like this. It was simple. It was just a simple function, which took bookings and views, and a random tiebreaker in case there were two hotels which had the same rank. The formula evolved over time. We introduced cancellations. It was taking consideration of seasonality. What is the distance of the hotel from the center? What is the number of views the hotel is getting?

Availability of the hotel. The average ranking in the locality. What is the visitor traffic? Guest reviews. These are just some flavors of what are the factors we considered. Back then, ranking actually was computed offline using simple Perl cron scripts every night, and then the scores were dumped into MySQL, and we used it in real time. Around 2016, we actually tried to replace the ranking formula with machine learning, and we failed miserably. The handcrafted formula was undefeatable. We could not beat it for a long time, like one and a half years or so. This formula cannot be beaten. The reasons were many fold. The primary reason was that the ideal model that we wanted to train the model on, and the massive amount of data that we had was not actually helpful when Spark kept exploding. The memory of Spark was not sufficient. What we did was we cut corners, we made some approximations, and we succeeded. In true Booking sense, we ran an experiment, and it was successful.

Next, we wanted to tackle personalized ranking, and there was a problem. This is what it looked like. The ranking scores was calculated offline until then. It was put into MySQL, and an availability engine read that MySQL data, loaded it into memory. The responsibility of this availability engine was that it needs to search the availability and prices of millions of properties. Because of the amount of data that this engine had, it used a scatter-gather pattern. It had a coordinator and 24 shards. Each of those shards actually worked on a subset of the data. When a request came in from the user, it came to the availability engine via a search orchestrator, and the request landed there. The request contained something like this. Where does the user want to search on? When? Then, what is the party size? Then, what are the filters and preferences of the user?

The coordinator accepted that request and then distributed the work to the workers. Workers went on to do their job. They actually looked into the subset of the data that they had, took the data out, and then they used the ranking scores that were preloaded into memory to do the sorting. After they did the sorting, they supplied the results back to the coordinator. Coordinator aggregated all the information from the workers and re-sorted the results and gave the results back to the search. This is what was happening. If you wanted to personalize, meaning that every user gets a specific set of results, what we had to do was take the ranking logic out of this availability engine, get rid of those static scores at the bottom, and then replace it with a service. Then have that service invoke actually a model which is deployed in the model serving platform that we saw earlier.

That's what we wanted to do. There were two problems. The first problem was, if there were 1,000 requests for the availability engine, it meant that the new service is going to get 24,000 requests because it was sitting behind the fanout, behind the shards. Secondly, the availability engine was operating at super low latency, and that also meant that this new service plus the network hop to the model and the model's time all needs to be well within the time of that service. It's basically a high throughput, low latency problem, and we managed to crack it. These are the numbers from 2024. That ranking service that you saw in the previous slide, that green box that was introduced new, is able to solve 100,000 requests per second with a p99.9 latency of 100 milliseconds. The average is way low. It's like 40, 50 milliseconds or so.

I want to share one more thing before I wrap up the evolution story. Experiments at Booking typically run for two to four weeks, but this meant that we couldn't actually train or run models. We were limited in the number of models that we can run every year, because we just had 53 weeks. We wanted to move faster, knowing well that if we actually put in a bad ranking model upfront, it is going to cost all of us, like travelers, partners, and business. What we did was we introduced interleaving. This is how it worked. Typically, for an A/B testing, we actually take the users and split them across two groups, and then we show different search results for them, which was coming from different ranking models. In interleaving, what we did was we didn't show two groups, we didn't split the groups, we just showed the same results for all users.

Those results were coming from merged data, meaning we would train a couple of models, in this case, two models, red and blue. We trained the model, and each of these models gave a list of results. Then we would somehow need to merge it. One simple example could be, take the top one from here, top one from here, merge it. Then keep alternating it. It's just a team draft approach. Then once you have done, you present that to all users across the service. Then you check offline, ok, from which list did the user interact more? Was it from model A or from model B? That gives us the answer. Why it was useful was we could suddenly run more variants. On the right side, it doesn't have to be two. We can even run eight different models that are actually interleaving the results for search. That is, we can run more variants that was like 10 times speed-up than what we are used to with A/B testing.

We could use it with less traffic because interleaving is super sensitive to customer preferences, and we can get signals faster. The way we use it now, interleaving and A/B, is that we train a bunch of models, we pre-select it with interleaving, we pick up a winner, and then we take the winner and then do proper A/B testing. We have optimized both speed, while not losing scientific rigor.

I started the talk by saying that experiment laid the foundation in general for data-driven decision-making. You can see that, still, it continues to underpin what we do every day. With that, that concludes the evolution story.

What's Brewing?

Next, I want to tell you where we are going. These are the five platforms that you saw. What we started doing last year is that we started building the foundations of agentic systems. By agentic systems, think about memories, all kinds of memories, episodic, semantic, procedural, and think about agent serving, like access control for those agents, delegation controls for the users to those agents, agent-to-agent communication. Those are the things we started working on last year. Parallelly, what we are also doing is unifying all these platforms under a single umbrella and then having a single orchestration layer. Why? Because we foresee a possible fragmentation and we wanted to avoid it earlier. Like for cross-domain use cases, we want a single, centralized, unified experience for the customer, and this platform can do that. Secondly, we wanted to centralize all kinds of AI-related governance, security, quality, and all those things. We wanted to centralize that.

See more presentations with transcripts

entries.title: Vercel Releases UI SDK for Agents to Compose UI from Reusable Behaviors
entries.summary: Vercel has released UI SDK in beta, an Apache 2.0 TypeScript library of more than 50 UI behaviors in @ui-sdk/core, with adapters for React, Vue, Svelte, Solid, and Web Components, so agents can compose accessible components and operate them through a documented agent bridge. By Daniel Dominguez
entries.content:
Vercel has released UI SDK, an open-source TypeScript library that treats keyboard navigation, focus, selection, popups, and drag and drop as reusable behaviors rather than details buried inside finished components. Vercel UI SDK is published on GitHub as vercel-labs/ui and is currently in beta.

The behaviors live in @ui-sdk/core. Vercel says it built more than 50 of them, including createPopup, createSelection, createTypeahead, createRovingFocus, createReorder, createResize, createViewport, createListbox, createChange, createFocusRecovery, and createVirtualizer. A developer, or more often an agent, combines those helpers inside definePrimitive, which declares a component's state, API, and slots once. Framework adapters then render the same primitive through createParts in React, Vue, Svelte, Solid, or as Web Components. The parts are unstyled and expose attributes and CSS variables. The same behaviors also back a starter library of more than 50 unstyled components, from Color Picker, Token Input, and Command to Calendar, Tree, and OTP Input, with the same part names in all five adapters.

UI SDK is meant to be used by agents, not only written by them. The ui-sdk skill, installed with npx skills add vercel-labs/ui --skill ui-sdk, points an agent at the Markdown docs shipped in the installed packages. At runtime, createAgent, imported from the matching framework package such as @ui-sdk/react/agent, exposes snapshot, act, and query so an agent can read component state and call actions through the component API, without screenshots. Apps can approve or refuse those steps, and change callbacks receive a source of "agent" and may cancel a change. registerTools can expose the same methods to a browser's built-in agent through WebMCP, when the browser provides document.modelContext.

Developers already have several headless libraries at this layer, including Radix UI, Base UI, React Aria, Ark UI and its Zag.js state machines, and Headless UI. shadcn/ui sits one level above those primitives as a copy-into-your-repo component kit. UI SDK aims lower, at composable behaviors shared across frameworks, and adds a first-class agent bridge. The changelog thanks the teams behind Radix, Base UI, React Aria, shadcn/ui, Nuxt UI, and Geist. Vercel has not said whether shadcn/ui will be rebuilt on UI SDK.

Rahim, a product engineer at Mux who built Vidstack, wrote after reading the source:

This is so genuinely cool. I love how it's been packaged up. So elegant @shadcn and @shuding! I'll be studying this for a while. 1. createAgent is an "agent bridge" which gives a snapshot, act, and query tool. It allows agents to interact with the actual UI components directly 2. Change callbacks know when the agent made the change (details.source === "agent"), and the app can refuse it with cancel (I love this)

A developer identified as Stefan looked at the repository and asked how the idea compares with existing headless libraries:

I tried looking at the repo a bit but I’m not sure I quite understand the value prop of this versus something like Base UI. Is the thought process that we should be thinking about UIs/components as combinations of behaviours?

UI SDK is in beta as 0.1.0-beta.1, licensed under the Apache License 2.0, and subject to Vercel's public beta terms; the APIs, documentation, and behavior may change before general availability. Install @ui-sdk/core plus the adapter for your framework, for example npm install @ui-sdk/react @ui-sdk/core, which requires React 19 or later. The Vue, Svelte, and Solid adapters document peer ranges of Vue 3.5, Svelte 5.33, and Solid 2 from 2.0.0-rc.14. Setup details are in the documentation.

entries.title: AWS PrivateLink Tunnel Endpoints Open a Whole CIDR Range to Another Account
entries.summary: AWS has detailed tunnel endpoints, a PrivateLink endpoint type that gives a consumer VPC access to an entire network segment in another account rather than one resource at a time, over an overlapping address space and with consumer-initiated connections only. The consumer must wrap traffic in GENEVE; only TCP and DNS pass, and access logs cannot attribute traffic to a workload behind the endpoint.
entries.content:
AWS has published a technical walkthrough of tunnel endpoints, a VPC endpoint type launched in September that lets an application in one VPC reach every address in a CIDR range shared from another account, instead of one resource at a time. The provider shares a CIDR-type resource configuration through AWS Resource Access Manager and the consumer creates a tunnel endpoint against it. From then on, anything inside the range is reachable, including resources that did not exist when the share was made.

Bruce Pinsky and Ashish Kumar of AWS frame it as a vendor-access problem, for "a vendor or service provider whose software must reach applications and resources in a customer's network." Until now, that meant a separate PrivateLink resource configuration per database or host, which breaks down when the resources are ephemeral, or the customer does not want to enumerate them. With a CIDR configuration, the customer defines a perimeter in address ranges, and "resources located outside the perimeter can't be reached by the vendor." Two further properties come with the design: the consumer and provider VPCs can use overlapping CIDR blocks, and connections "can start only from the consumer VPC, not from the provider network."

(Source: AWS Networking & Content Delivery blog)

On the r/aws thread about the September launch, the first question was what this does that VPC peering does not, from a self-described veteran of AWS's advanced networking components. The answers that followed are the use cases: a peering connection exposes the whole VPC in both directions, while a tunnel endpoint shares a subset of the address space in one direction only; one commenter at a bank wrote that "peering with unregulated partners is a massive no-no, the auditors will rip you to shreds for it." Another pointed to clusters that do client-side load balancing, such as self-managed Kafka or Aerospike, which until now needed port-based routing on a Network Load Balancer and a separate port-mapping horizon for connections arriving over an interface endpoint. The same thread drew the line against VPC Lattice itself: Lattice services work at layer 7, tunnel endpoints at layer 4 without a resource configuration per target.

The unusual part is on the consumer side: the application's traffic has to arrive at the tunnel endpoint wrapped in GENEVE, the encapsulation protocol defined in RFC 8926, over UDP port 6081 and in the same Availability Zone. The endpoint strips the header, checks that the inner destination falls inside the shared range, rewrites the source to a resource gateway address, and forwards a plain packet into the provider VPC. Linux can do the wrapping in the kernel. The walkthrough creates an ip link add ... type geneve id 0 device inside its own network namespace with a default route through it, which sends the provider's ranges into the tunnel and leaves the instance's other traffic alone. On the far side, the resources see the resource gateway as the client, so the post advises security groups that reference the gateway's security group or subnet rather than a single address.

The documentation lists the constraints. Inner traffic must be TCP, with UDP permitted only for DNS, so ICMP and ping do not work, and IP fragments are dropped. Private DNS names are not supported on tunnel endpoints. The endpoint's subnets must sit in Availability Zones that overlap with the resource gateway's, or the association shows as inaccessible. A resource gateway's DNS setting cannot be changed after creation. And the access logs identify the consumer's endpoint but carry no field for the inner source address, so a provider can attribute traffic to a vendor and not to a workload behind that vendor's endpoint. The post also warns that sharing 0.0.0.0/0 grants access to everything the provider VPC can route to, including networks behind VPC peering, Direct Connect or a Site-to-Site VPN, and recommends sharing the narrowest ranges that work.

Both points have been tested in practice. Ryo Suzuki of the Japanese consultancy Classmethod connected two VPCs that both use 10.0.0.0/16 and got HTTP through, but only by running a GENEVE relay as root on the client, by routing a /32 per destination host, or by putting an HAProxy or NAT instance in front, each of which adds a hop or a single point of failure; his conclusion was that "route management according to the number of destinations is required." In a second experiment, he shared 0.0.0.0/0 from a VPC with a NAT gateway and reached the internet from a VPC with no gateway at all, which confirmed AWS's warning from the other side; he judged it workable as a temporary path and "difficult to use in a permanent production setup."

Pricing is an hourly charge per tunnel endpoint plus a per-GB charge for data processed, under PrivateLink pricing, with the provider side billed per GB through the resource gateway under VPC Lattice pricing, and the feature is available in 28 regions. Terraform support followed from the community: a contributor request opened two days after launch was implemented by another contributor and shipped in version 6.71.0 of the AWS provider, as a Tunnel endpoint type on aws_vpc_endpoint and a cidr_resource block on the Lattice resource configuration.

entries.title: Yelp Migrates Cassandra to EKS by Moving EBS Volumes
entries.summary: Yelp has moved its Cassandra fleet from legacy self-managed Kubernetes clusters to Amazon EKS by re-pointing existing EBS volumes at new pods, rather than streaming data between nodes. By Claudio Masolo
entries.content:
Yelp has moved its Cassandra fleet from legacy self-managed Kubernetes clusters to Amazon EKS by re-pointing existing EBS volumes at new pods, rather than streaming data between nodes. A blog post by the site reliability team details a migration. It covered about 90 production clusters. There was zero downtime for customers and no data loss. The largest cluster, a 54-pod user-data store, took about 12 hours end to end.

Yelp had already moved its stateless workloads to EKS through its PaaSTA deployment layer, but Cassandra stayed behind. Kubernetes has no built-in way to migrate 

StatefulSets
and their persistent volumes across clusters. The usual approach is to add nodes to the new cluster and shut down the old ones. This would temporarily double compute capacity but also lead to data transfer costs. For the largest clusters, streaming alone could have taken weeks. Yelp also considered a regional failover and rebuild, and a new Cassandra datacenter in EKS, but rated both as less transparent to customers.

Yelp's "Rolling PV Transplant" relies on the fact that an EBS volume is bound to an Availability Zone, not to a Kubernetes cluster, and that a 

PersistentVolume
is effectively a pointer to a volume ID. The team pre-creates PVs and PVCs in EKS that reference the existing volume IDs, then creates an identical 
StatefulSet
there, whose pods wait in 
ContainerCreating
. The automation then deletes one pod at a time on the legacy cluster, waits for the volume to detach, and lets the EKS pod claim it. The pod rejoins the ring with the same data and token range, and the process repeats for the next pod. Cassandra's replication tolerates the few minutes each node is offline.

Yelp set a 

skipReconciliation: true
flag on the custom resources in both clusters. This was done because two operators managed the same logical ring during the migration. The flag helped prevent them from conflicting over pod state. The flag was cleared on the EKS side at the end.

Across roughly 1,000 pods, about 1,000 TiB moved by pointer rather than over the wire. No node was ever decommissioned from the ring, so rollback was the same operation in reverse. Yelp used it a handful of times, for a missing subnet definition and a certificate mismatch, and restored pods within minutes. After a week of manual dev runs and a week of automation, one engineer ran the production rollout in about three weeks, migrating three to six clusters on a typical day.

The team had Claude generate the orchestration script, roughly 800 lines of bash, from its validated manual runbook, rather than asking it to design the procedure. The script needed minor adjustments after two days of testing.

The approach relies on a previous Container Storage Interface migration by Yelp's Compute Infrastructure team. This work gave the Data Infrastructure team confidence in the volume detach and attach process. Yelp also used the technique for Kafka clusters, and says it applies to any AZ-pinned stateful workload on Kubernetes. The legacy clusters are now retired.

The one failure specific to this technique was a stale 

VolumeAttachment
object left behind by the AWS CSI controller after pod deletion. The EKS pod sat in Pending with no error, and deleting the object on the legacy cluster fixed it. Yelp advises building explicit timeouts for stalled detach and attach operations into any automation. Two other findings were unrelated to the mechanism. Backups failed with IAM AccessDenied errors for 48 hours because a new -eks role was not yet being assumed by scheduled jobs, and the alert only filed a ticket instead of paging. Pausing repairs for the migration also exposed one cluster whose repairs had been silently disabled for three months, leaving accumulated data inconsistencies. Teams planning a similar move should audit repair state, backup IAM roles and alert severity before starting.

Yelp's approach is not the only way to move Cassandra between EKS clusters. Monday.com's engineering team describes a different one in a post on zero-downtime Cassandra migration between EKS clusters. K8ssandra-managed clusters had to move without any downtime or data loss. So, the team created a workflow to add new Cassandra data centers, safely transfer data, and remove the old ones. That is the streaming model Yelp considered and rejected. The new cluster is brought up alongside the old one and receives data over the network, and the original is retired only afterwards. The team believes success relied more on control, automation, and handling failures than on speed. They automated long tasks like rebuilds and planned the migration in stages based on operator behavior.

The two migrations differ in what they trade away. Yelp's disk transplant skips data transfer and extra compute. It allows for a rollback by swapping the pointer. However, it relies on EBS volumes being linked to an Availability Zone, not a cluster. Monday.com's approach does not rely on that property, and it keeps the old environment intact until the end. The cost is a longer migration and the capacity to run both sides at once, which Yelp calculated would have taken weeks for its largest clusters.

Despite the different mechanics, the post-migration lessons are similar. Monday.com devotes part of its write-up to verifying that backups work after the migration, along with monitoring, dashboards and alerts. Yelp's own backups failed on an IAM role mismatch within 48 hours of its first production clusters landing in EKS. Teams planning either approach should treat those checks as part of the migration plan, not as cleanup afterwards.

entries.title: How Shopify Orchestrates AI-Powered Mobile App Development without Overloading Developers' Machines
entries.summary: To prevent AI development workflows from exhausting developer machines' resources, Shopify built Remote Dev, a remote mobile development environment that enables AI agents to independently build, test and maintain iOS and Android applications and in parallel. By Sergio De Simone
entries.content:
To prevent AI development workflows from exhausting developer machines' resources, Shopify built Remote Dev, a remote mobile development environment that enables AI agents to independently build, test and maintain iOS and Android applications and in parallel.

In fact, according to Shopify engineers, running agentic workflows in parallel quickly hogs all resources available on development machines. They explain that "three or four workflows were enough to max out a laptop", on top of the resources already consumed by compilers, simulators, and emulators. Moreover, "if someone accidentally closed a laptop lid, the work stopped".

Shopify had previously built River to address the same challenge in web and backend development, but, being River a Linux-based solution, it could not be used for building iOS apps. To overcome this limitation, Shopify built Remote Dev:

With Remote Dev, we're no longer limited by how many builds and simulators our laptops can handle. Each River session gets its own environment, so we can have one agent debugging something on Android, another working on an iOS feature, and another testing a PR, all in parallel.

Remote Dev uses a fleet of remote Macs running Shopify's development environment and iOS simulators, accessible via SSH. Android emulators run on separate Linux VMs. This architecture allows developers to build and test both iOS and Android builds through the same SSH session.

Agents can work on multiple tasks in parallel, each with its own environment for maximum independence. They can also be accessed through a Slack channel backed by River. Thanks to this setup, Remote Dev can

implement changes, build the app, run tests, interact with the simulators, collect screenshots, and create a PR. If something fails, it can inspect the logs, fix the issue, and try again, all while we focus on other tasks.

The platform supports automated workflows, including overnight runs that identify bugs, implement fixes, and submit PRs. Agents can also verify that a build is functional by navigating through the app, interacting with its UI, reproducing bugs, recording current behavior, implementing fixes, and running the same interaction to verify the fix.

Shopify says that, after promoting internal adoption through demonstrations and storytelling, River's share of merged PRs increased from 6% to 61%.

Commenting on Shopify's article, LinkedIn user Raiyan Jugbhery, in charge of software infrastructure and founder at SpendMe, argued that the key advantage of Remove Dev is its Xcode and iOS Simulator integration, noting that "a PR you still have to pull and verify on a Mac isn't really autonomous". However, he pointed out that the article does not explain "how they keep builds from queuing when several agents ask for a Mac at once", which he identified as a key concern.

Junaid Raza, solutions architect at Hoboetech, raised another concern. Allowing agents to run the simulator could lead to unreliable test results, as "give [the agent] a red test and enough retries and it'll sometimes rewrite the test until it passes". To prevent this, he suggests prohibiting runner agents from modifying the tests they execute.

Shopify says it plans to expand the platform with continuous application health monitoring, automated crash detection and fixes, and PR generation for identified issues, among other capabilities.

entries.title: Qwik 2.0 RC: Replaces HTML Comment Markers for Faster Reactivity and Out-of-Order Streaming
entries.summary: Qwik 2.0 Release Candidate, published on 1 October 2026, replaces v1's HTML comment markers with two script blocks that hold state and virtual node data. It adds experimental out-of-order streaming, async useComputed$, and cacheable route loaders. Qwik's benchmarks show v2 at 1.23x vanilla JavaScript, versus 2.59x for v1. A migration command is provided. By Daniel Curtis
entries.content:
Qwik, the resumable JavaScript framework originally created at Builder.io, has released its 2.0 Release Candidate, targeting a rewrite of how the framework encodes resumable state in server-rendered HTML and introducing experimental out-of-order streaming. The RC was published on 1st October 2026 as 

@qwik.dev/core@2.0.0-rc.0
, around two years and eight months after the initial Towards Qwik 2.0 design article.

In v1, Qwik propagated state updates by sprinkling HTML comment markers such as

and
throughout the rendered body to flag component boundaries and the text nodes a signal should update. That approach forced a single ordered write pass, added CPU and memory overhead, and made out-of-order streaming impossible because a slow fetch blocked everything after it. In v2 the comments are gone, with state and virtual node information instead compressed into two 
<script
and 
<script
blocks at the end of the document.

On Qwik's internal runs of js-framework-benchmark, v2 posts a weighted geometric mean of 1.23 times slower than vanilla JavaScript, ahead of Vue 3.5 at 1.25x, Angular 22 at 1.42x, React 19 with the compiler at 1.53x, and v1 itself at 2.59x. A detailed classmethod walkthrough that built the same starter against both versions reported server-rendered HTML went from 60 comments to zero, with JavaScript required before interactivity dropping from 59KB to 9KB, though total bundle size grew.

Out-of-order HTML streaming has also been added in experimental mode. Developers can wrap slow regions in

and
boundaries so the server sends the rest of the page immediately and streams the real content later in the same response, with a small inline script swapping it into place. The APIs are opt-in through 
vite.config.ts
:
qwikVite({ experimental: ['pendingBoundary', 'catchBoundary', 'blockSSR'] })


useComputed$
now accepts async functions, replacing
, and route loaders gain their own JSON endpoints with 
cacheControl
and 
eTag
options so the browser can cache them individually and 
<Link
can prefetch data on hover. Other additions include a 
worker$
primitive for Web Workers, 
reactify$
for embedding Qwik components inside React trees, server-only 
*.server.ts
files, and HMR that preserves signal and store values across edits.

In a Reddit discussion predating the v2 RC, one developer called the lack of out-of-order streaming a significant limitation and argued that the Qwik team should be more upfront about it. Another commenter suggested that streaming could be a future feature. In his Classmethod walkthrough, Hiroshi Morishige noted the long wait for v2, it reached alpha in November 2024 and beta in June 2025, while v1 continued to receive updates through 1.20.1 in September 2026. He also noted that SvelteKit 3 and Remix 3.0 released stable versions on the same day as Qwik's RC, with the three releases published within seven hours. Qwik 2 and SvelteKit 3 use Vite 8; Remix 3 is independent of Vite.

The team says the breaking changes are small and automated by 

pnpm qwik migrate-v2
, which also handles the move to the new 
@qwik.dev/core
and 
@qwik.dev/router
package names. New projects can scaffold with 
pnpm create qwik@rc
, and the RC can be explored via next.qwik.dev/examples or the online playground.

Qwik is an open-source resumable framework that serialises state and event listeners into HTML, then lazily loads component JavaScript only in response to user interaction. The project is MIT licensed and developed openly on GitHub.

entries.title: Datadog Brings Production Experimentation to AI Agent Observability
entries.summary: Datadog is extending its Agent Observability platform with Online Experiments, allowing engineering teams to compare AI agent versions against real production traffic rather than relying exclusively on predefined evaluation datasets. By Craig Risi
entries.content:
Datadog is extending its Agent Observability platform with Online Experiments, allowing engineering teams to compare AI agent versions against real production traffic rather than relying exclusively on predefined evaluation datasets. The capability combines agent evaluation scores with operational measurements such as latency, token consumption, execution cost, and errors, helping teams establish whether changes to models, prompts, retrieval strategies, or tools actually improve an agent.

The announcement addresses a growing challenge in agent development: a change that performs better in a controlled test may behave very differently when exposed to unpredictable user requests. Datadog's approach brings controlled experimentation, production telemetry, and execution traces together, giving teams evidence of both the outcome and the behaviour behind it.

Offline evaluations remain an important part of agent development. Teams can run different versions against predefined datasets, assess responses and identify known regressions before deployment.

However, these evaluations are only as representative as the datasets and scoring criteria behind them. New user workflows, unexpected requests, and changing tool responses can expose weaknesses that existing test cases never anticipated.

Online experiments address this limitation by evaluating agent behaviour against real user interactions. Teams can compare a control version with a modified variant by randomly distributing production traffic between them, reducing the influence of differences in user requests.

This provides a more realistic view of how an agent performs under actual workloads, while also helping teams identify new scenarios that should eventually become part of their offline regression datasets.

Datadog integrates its Agent Observability evaluators with its Experiments capability, allowing evaluation scores to be compared alongside conventional operational metrics.

Teams can measure response quality, accuracy, and completeness while tracking execution duration, token consumption, estimated cost, and workflow errors. Feature Flags manage traffic allocation, letting engineers expose a change to a small percentage of users before rolling it out more widely.

This is important because improvements rarely come without trade-offs. A cheaper model might require more retries, while a revised retrieval strategy could improve evidence quality but increase execution time.

Datadog also connects experiment results to individual agent traces. Engineers can inspect tool calls, supplied arguments, and returned results to understand why a particular variant behaved differently.

According to the article, the experiment compared GPT-5.6 Luna against GPT-6 Luna, splitting traffic evenly between the two. An LLM-based evaluator scored investigation quality from one to five, considering accuracy, completeness, and whether conclusions were supported by available evidence.

They claim the results showed a 44.3% reduction in estimated cost for the newer model, with quality scores remaining close at 3.84 and 3.86, respectively.

However, the operational results revealed potential concerns. The newer model showed estimated increases in execution duration and workflow errors, although the confidence intervals were too broad to establish definitive regressions.

Inspecting the traces revealed that the newer model also supplied invalid tool parameters more frequently, usually recovering after retries. This behaviour was not sufficiently visible in the overall quality score.

Datadog used that finding to improve tool handling before proceeding with the model change. The failed calls also provided candidates for additional offline regression tests.

Datadog is not alone in trying to solve this challenge. Tools such as LangSmith and Langfuse provide agent tracing and evaluation capabilities, while experimentation platforms such as LaunchDarkly support controlled feature rollouts. Datadog's approach connects these concerns within its existing observability ecosystem, linking evaluation results directly to production experiments and execution evidence.

Datadog's broader proposition is that online experiments can create a feedback loop between production behaviour and development testing. Unexpected failures become new regression cases, while subsequent experiments establish whether changes actually resolve them.

The important shift is from asking whether an agent passes a predefined evaluation to establishing whether it performs better under real conditions. For agent engineering, production experimentation may become as important as traditional software testing.

entries.title: Production AI, Architecture Trade-Offs & Team Design: InfoQ Opens Registration for 6 January Cohorts
entries.summary: From agent reliability to architecture decisions and delivery bottlenecks, InfoQ’s January 2027 cohorts give senior practitioners five weeks to examine current challenges, test approaches in their own work, and compare results with peers. By Artenisa Chatziou
entries.content:
InfoQ has opened registration for six online cohort workshops starting between January 9 and 22, 2027. Covering AI Engineering, Software Architecture, and High-Performing Teams, the five-week programs bring senior engineers, architects, and engineering leaders together to work through technical and organizational decisions with experienced practitioners.

The workshops go beyond studying technical material. Participants apply frameworks from QCon and InfoQ to decisions from their own work, compare approaches with practitioners from other organizations, and return to discuss what they tried and learned. Working across different organizational contexts helps expose trade-offs and assumptions that may not emerge from an internal discussion alone.

Each cohort combines four hours of live facilitated sessions per week, independent application work, and a program-specific capstone.

AI Engineering: Retrieval, Agents, and Evaluation

Production AI involves decisions beyond model selection: how context is retrieved and maintained, how much autonomy agents should have, and how reliability, latency, and inference costs are managed.

The InfoQ AI Engineering Program examines these decisions through RAG architectures, agent design, platforms, and evaluation. Participants work through technical approaches and failure modes, applying them to AI systems or proposals from their own work.

Three January cohorts are planned:

  • Hien Luu, AI/ML leader and author of MLOps with Ray, starts January 9, Saturdays at 09:00 PST.
  • Adi Polak, director of developer experience engineering at Confluent, starts January 21, Thursdays at 08:00 PST.
  • Lan Chu, principal engineer at Rabobank and author of Post-training LLMs, starts January 22, Fridays at 14:00 CET. Her QCon London 2026 presentation examined a production RAG system built on more than 10,000 documents and used by more than 300 people.

Architecture: Decisions across Teams and Platforms

Architecture choices are shaped by system requirements, team boundaries, platform ownership, and organizational constraints.

The InfoQ Architect Program covers distributed systems, decentralized decisions, platform engineering, and AI architecture. Participants apply the material to architecture decisions they currently own, compare trade-offs with peers, and practice communicating their reasoning to stakeholders.

The capstone involves co-authoring a technical article examining AI's role in software architecture or platform engineering. Selected articles may be published on InfoQ.

Both cohorts start January 22 and are facilitated by Luca Mezzalira, independent software architect and author of Building Micro-Frontends. Friday sessions are offered at 09:30 GMT and 10:00 EST.

High-Performing Teams: Delivery Flow, Ownership, and AI

Faster coding does not necessarily improve delivery when reviews, approvals, or infrastructure dependencies become the constraint. AI agents also change how responsibilities are divided and which work requires human judgment.

The InfoQ High-Performing Teams Program examines team structure, ownership, delivery flow, AI responsibilities, and engineering metrics as one operating model.

Participants evaluate constraints in their own team environments, compare approaches with peers, and develop a proposed target operating model covering responsibilities, workflow, and measurement.

The January 12 cohort is facilitated by Olimpiu Pop, InfoQ Podcast co-host with experience in solutions architecture, engineering management, and CTO roles. Sessions run on Tuesdays and Thursdays, from 16:00 to 18:00 CET.

Workshop Format and Participation

The live online workshops focus on discussion and application rather than recorded lectures. Participants work with an experienced facilitator and a small cross-company peer group, bringing current engineering decisions into the sessions and testing approaches between meetings.

Sessions are not recorded, allowing participants to discuss organizational constraints more openly. Certification requires attendance, active participation, and successful completion of the program capstone.

Participation costs USD $1,470 per person. Full schedules, syllabi, and registration details are available on the InfoQ Online Certification Programs website.
